newsitem.title: RUSSIA: World Bank to lend Russia $800 mln for reform-Tass.
newsitem.headline: World Bank to lend Russia $800 mln for reform-Tass.

text.p: The World Bank has agreed to lend Russia $800 million to help it reform its social security system, Itar-Tass news agency quoted a World Bank official as saying in Moscow on Monday.
Russian officials and representatives of the Washington-based institution were not immediately available for comment. Moscow ministers had previously said they were hoping for a $600 million credit.

Tass quoted Andrei Markov, an official at the World Bank's representative office in Moscow, as saying the loan, the biggest the Bank has extended to Russia, would be paid out in three tranches of $300, $200 and $300 million, with the second amount conditional on the government paying what it owes to pensioners.

The government is struggling with huge shortfalls in tax revenues and massive arrears in the payment of pensions and other benefits in a Soviet-era welfare system which First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais described last week as "fantastically inefficient".
Chubais, who has spearheaded economic reforms since being appointed three months ago, has vowed to cut out waste and put the system on a sound footing.

The first tranche of World Bank funds would go directly towards helping pay off the government's pension debt, Tass said. Ministers have pledged to wipe out the pension arrears worth hundreds of millions of dollars by July 1.

The first funds from the World Bank loan, which Markov said was agreed on Saturday with Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev, would arrive in the next weeks, following a meeting of the Bank's board at the end of June.
If the pension arrears were paid off, the second tranche would follow in December and the third early next year.

The Bank's loan is also intended to further the development of private pension funds to reduce the burden on the Russian state, as well as reform unemployment and childcare benefits and other aspects of the social security system.
In addition, the World Bank will lend Moscow $30 million to pay for technical assistance on its welfare schemes, notably to purchase an annual outside audit of the state pension fund.

Tass quoted Markov as saying that a 1996 state audit of the fund would be completed in 1998 and that government measures this year to prepare the fund for auditing would also determine the fate of the second tranche of its credit.

Russia is in its second year of receiving regular payments of a $10-billion three-year loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Several tranches have been delayed this year and last over worries about Moscow's ability to control its budget.
